Row 363: an `asDebugString` that prints as walk's does, where the compiled one prints `Box`. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. Once the compiled path reads the one library, every object inherits such a member, the `getter toString` of that library's `trait Object`, so every object with no `asString` meets the overflow.
98	
99	### The specification's revision
100	
101	- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
102	- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
103	- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
104	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
105	
106	### The suites and the gate
107	
108	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
109	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
110	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
111	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
112	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.

<!-- The POSITIONS provenance audit of 2026-10-21 and 22: what it is, where its parts are, and how to run its mining workflow again. -->

# The POSITIONS provenance audit

The audit asks of each POSITIONS entry whether it is the curator's decision, faithfully recorded, or an agent's summary or default that readers took as his word. It ran as a trial on ten entries (`trial/`) and then on the other 75 (`full/`); its corrections are applied at `6b560762f`. Its evidence feeds the clarity workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/`).

## The mining workflow

`full/evidence/workflow.js`: per chunk of ten entries, a Sonnet scout per entry (archaeology only), an Opus judgement, an Opus writer on a copy of the record, a cold read and a takeaway check. Its briefs are `full/evidence/briefs/` (the writer's rules 0 to 12); its scripts are `tools/` (`leads.py N` gathers an entry's trail in about 2.5 seconds; `tests.py` checks them; `hischeck.py` checks a report's block of the curator's quotes).

To run it again on entries it has not traced, copy the briefs to a new evidence folder and change the report paths in them, then run the script with that folder and `args: { chunks: [{ name, entries: [numbers] }] }`; at most two agents run at once in one Workflow, so run several side by side. Its results: `full/RESULTS.md`. Today's clarity workflow merges the writer's two passes: the correction by the audit's rules and the rewrite for clarity can be one writer stage when the mining runs again.
<!-- The POSITIONS audit's full run on the 75 entries the trial did not trace, 2026-10-21 to 22: what it proposes, grouped by type for the curator's approval (50 entries change, 25 kept word for word), its 16 questions, its checks and its cost; the reports, judgements, proposals and checks of its eight chunks are in evidence/. Nothing is applied. -->

# The full run's results

Eight chunks of POSITIONS, 75 entries, from 23:37 UTC on 2026-10-21 to 02:25 UTC on 10-22, in four Workflow runs of two chunks each. Each chunk: a Sonnet scout per entry (`evidence/P-N.md`), an Opus judgement (`judgement-cN.md`), an Opus writer on a copy of the record (`corrections-cN.md`, `corrections-cN.apply`, `rewritten-cN.txt`, `review-queue-items-cN.md`), a cold read (`cold-read-cN.md`) and a takeaway check (`takeaway-cN.md`). The briefs are in `evidence/briefs/`, the script in `evidence/workflow.js`. Nothing in POSITIONS, FACTS or their histories has changed.

## What it proposes, by group

The page https://claude.ai/artifact/XSW5Pz56938NcmCPg4GMZb (version 10; group 7 in version 11) shows each entry's change and its whole text before and after.

1. Status and counts moved to the history (8): P-45, P-50, P-51, P-89, P-147, P-149, P-152, P-155.
2. Factual errors corrected (12): P-12, P-19, P-28, P-47, P-53, P-69, P-70, P-72, P-74, P-87, P-91, P-102.
3. One-time approvals and remarks struck (6): P-8, P-9, P-33, P-44, P-78, P-79.
4. Defaults moved to the review queue (8): P-17, P-30, P-40, P-57, P-60, P-75, P-146, P-153.
5. Reworded back to his meaning (10): P-29, P-32, P-39, P-46, P-48, P-54, P-56, P-58, P-62, P-154.
6. Struck (2): P-16, P-123; F-39's pointer to P-123 is rewritten with it.
7. Handles from past conversations struck (19), added at his page comment on P-45 of 2026-10-22 04:53 UTC (`evidence/handles.apply`, applied after the eight): "answer N", "ask N", an "item N" of the questions of 10-09 whose number now names another review-queue item, a probe's "Q1". P-45's at his word, the other 18 the coordinator's proposal. Only P-52 and P-59 are in no other group; with them, 52 entries change and 23 are kept.
- Held for his answers (4): P-27, P-38, P-43, P-90.
- Kept word for word by the writers (25; group 7 would change P-52 and P-59): P-7, P-11, P-25, P-26, P-37, P-41, P-42, P-49, P-52, P-59, P-67, P-68, P-71, P-73, P-76, P-77, P-80, P-84, P-95, P-96, P-97, P-98, P-103, P-124, P-125. Each has source lines for its history that `record.py` cannot write (each chunk's "History lines" section).

Ten review-queue items are drafted for groups 4 and 5; one more (c8, P-124) only if he prefers it to his question. Sixteen questions: fourteen from the writers, on P-26, P-27, P-38, P-42, P-43 (two), P-59, P-77, P-87, P-90, P-95, P-123, P-124 and P-152, and P-85's two from the trial. The takeaway checks found 19 kept sentences that a reader with no context misread; by his rule of 23:21 UTC on 10-21 none is fixed, and each fix is drafted in its chunk's takeaway file.

## The checks

- `tools/hischeck.py` on the 75 reports and 8 judgements: 1,100 quotes of his, all EXACT.
- The eight apply files applied together, in chunk order, on one copy of the record (`scratchpad/positions-audit/full/combined/`), then `record.py check --base 6897e6f48`: 0 failures; POSITIONS from 83 entries to 81; 49 entries rewritten (48 of POSITIONS and F-39), 2 removed.
- The page's groups were checked by script against that copy: the 50 entries the groups name are exactly the 50 that change.

## Points for the next steps

- The writers found history blocks of the consolidation of 2026-10-13 that name the wrong commit (chunks c2, c3, c4 and c6). `record.py` cannot amend a block; the history-only command should cover them.
- "Built." in an entry with nothing left to build: chunks c4, c5, c6 and c8 kept the bare word by rule 0; c7 moved P-89's to the history. The coordinator proposes keeping it in P-89 too.
- Each writer's "The rules, where they fit badly" lists the cases where two rules of the brief pulled apart (mostly rule 0 against rules 2, 6 and 9).

## The cost

19.3M tokens written by the four runs (`tools/spend.py` from epoch 1792625800): 5.38M, 4.75M, 5.19M and 3.97M. The estimate was 16M to 17M. A VM restart at 00:03 UTC killed the runs; they were resumed at 00:05 with their finished agents reused, and the agents killed mid-work ran again from the start.

1	<!-- The evidence map for the top-tier review Pavol asked for on 2026-09-29, of whether his decisions since 2026-09-16 finish or depart from what Fortress's designers intended, written that day by an Opus worker, reading only, for the Fable judge who reads it and then the primary sources it cites. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's decisions since 2026-09-16: the evidence for the review
4	
5	## How to read this
6	
7	- Each entry has five parts: (1) what he decided, his words, what landed; (2) the designers' latest word; (3) the alternatives the record weighed; (4) what the decision set in motion; (5) the doubts on record.
8	- This is a map, not a verdict. Where the record itself reads a decision as finishing or departing, the entry says whose reading it is.
9	- The record is pinned at `be9a75b79` (main, 2026-09-29, 12:30 UTC). FACTS and PLAN are rewritten often; if a line has moved, search for the entry's title.
10	- Abbreviations:
11	  - POSITIONS = `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`; FACTS = `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`; PLAN = `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`; ledger = `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`.
12	  - `reviews/` = `explorations/reviews/`; `ladder/` = `explorations/compile-ladder/`; `coordinator/` = `explorations/coordinator/`.
13	  - WD = `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the unrevised Working Draft of 2011-02-02 (FACTS:143). Spec = `Specification/`, which the revival revises in place. Read WD for the designers' text.
14	  - Types = `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, Luchangco's unfinished 2012 restart (FACTS:145).
15	  - "Walk" is the interpreter; "the checker" is the compiled path's static type checker.
16	
17	### Four facts about the standard itself

The numeral decision (D21: the implementers' `IntLiteral`) beside the team's own warning in the one library ("Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals", `FortressBuiltin.fss:497-498`) and its compile-time folding. 1	<!-- The top-tier judgement Pavol asked for on 2026-09-29 (POSITIONS, 2026-09-29, 12:17 UTC): have his decisions since 2026-09-16 kept faith with what Fortress's designers and implementers intended and with his own principles, and has he committed a cardinal error of commission or of omission. Written the same day, reading only, from the evidence map `evidence.md` (`8b35d782b`) and from the primary sources it cites, each deciding claim checked at its line: `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (the Working Draft of February 2011), `Specification/` (the same draft as the revival revises it), `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` (the 2008 release, read through pdftotext), `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick` (the 2012 Types chapter), `Papers/Types/`, `Papers/Welterweight/`, the team's library and prelude, and the team's commits. Nothing was run, no Fortress program measured. Tree at `dd55a31ad`. For Pavol, who has not read the specification, the type papers or the library, and for the coordinator. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's decisions since 2026-09-16, judged against the designers' intent
4	
5	## In short
6	
7	- On every large call he has gone the way the designers' own implementers went: one library, the exclusion rule kept and the number tower flattened, sizes in the types with unboxed storage, the 2009 overload sentence dropped, `comprises` read at the level of values, conversions never changing which declaration runs. Each of these is what the type group built or wrote last, not what the early draft wished.
8	- Where the designers left no word, his calls are pragmatic, consistent with each other, and mostly in the library's own patterns. Two are not: row 330 (`floor` on a float returning an unbounded integer), decided on a premise route A then removed and against the library's consistent declaration; and the written `extends Object` bound of batch 7, which turned a compile-time refusal into a JVM crash the switch-over will meet (row 447).
9	- No cardinal error of commission. Row 330 has cost nothing yet and reverses for the price of one entry. Row 447 costs one code-generator rung and must land before the switch-over.
10	- The errors of omission are in the plan, not in the decisions: the switch-over (phase 4) is the largest and least designed piece; phase 5's collision between "no model line changes" and "sizes in the model's own types" is measured (decision D's diff: 21 lines out, 29 in) but not yet faced by him; the unboxed store's mechanism (decision A) has no design and the "fast" half of the goal rests on it.
11	- The standard itself has two voices on the tower, and his decisions follow the later one. The record's own brief for route A did not cite the sentence that most supports it (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:501-502`).
12	- He has not gone astray. Section 6 lists eleven things to decide or confirm, the first four before batch 7b.
13	
14	## 1. Primer: what the designers were aiming for
15	
16	Terms are defined where they first appear. "The team" is the Sun/Oracle Fortress group, 2003-2012. "Walk" is the interpreter; "the checker" is the static type checker, which runs only on the compiled path. "The one library" is the interpreter's library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`), which his decision of 2026-09-21 makes the library the compiler checks. "The prelude" is the compiler's own smaller library (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), to be deleted at "the switch-over", the day the compiled path reads the one library.
17	
18	### The three texts, and which is the designers' latest word
19	
20	- The 2008 release is `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, 262 pages, the team's own artefact (`403afbe0b`, 2008-03-31).
21	- The Working Draft is the LaTeX under `Specification/`. The team's last edit to its text is 2010-12-09 (`44e03b176`). Steele cloned it whole into `Specification-1.0-frozen/` on 2012-01-04, so the frozen directory is byte for byte the draft of 2011-02-02, not the 1.0 text; only the PDF beside it is 1.0 (`coordinator/spec-lineage.md` §§ 1-2, checked). "July 2012" on the revival's PDF is the date of a parentless import commit, chosen by the revival (`414b790e3`), not of any edit.
22	- The restart is `Documentation/Specification/`, begun 2012-02-20 by Luchangco, abandoned 2012-05-31 with most chapters empty. Its Types chapter (`Prose/Language/types.tick`, 1,056 lines) is fresh 2012 prose and the team's last word on types, exclusion and `comprises`. It has no chapter on static parameters, numbers, coercion beyond a relation, or the library.
23	- The papers: the OOPSLA 2011 type-system paper (`Papers/Types/`), Naden's 2012 journal text on the return-type rule (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`, last touched 2012-08-31, the project's last day), the Welterweight calculus (2012), the four patents filed 2012-08-31, and Steele's 2016 retrospective (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md`).
24	- So "the designers' latest word" is not one text. On types and the exclusion rule it is the 2012 Types chapter and Naden. On the library, static parameters, coercion, overloading resolution and the number chapters it is the Working Draft, whose text on those topics is 2008-2010. On what they actually made run, it is the code: the interpreter's library (2007-2012, never type-checked) and the compiler's prelude and checker (2009-2012).
25	
26	### Numbers and the tower
27	
28	- A **tower** is a chain of number types where each is a subtype of the next: an integer is a rational is a real. In the interpreter's library the team built exactly that in 2008: `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number`, and kept it to the end (`reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` § 7, commits `cfe16b43b`, `fca589bbb`). The library chapters of the Working Draft say the same in prose: ℤ "is a subtype of ℚ" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:28-29`) and the listing has `trait ℤ extends { ℚ, ℤ*, ... }` (`:195-196`); ℚ "is a subtype of ℝ" (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:36-37`).
29	- The types chapter of the same draft says the opposite: "Moreover, there are several simple standard numeric types. These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them." (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:500-502`, the list that follows names ℤ, ℕ, ℚ, ℝ, ℂ and every fixed width). That sentence is not in the text of the 2008 release (searched) and is in the draft by February 2011; the cut history does not date it more closely. The 2012 Types chapter keeps it word for word (`types.tick:977-980`). So the draft contradicts itself, and the later text sides with exclusion.
30	- The compiler side went flat in 2009, after a tower that stood from March to August. Chase, 2009-08-31: "ZZ32 is NOT a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64; this would be a good time to get coercion working" (`6896886fb`). Maessen, 2009-11-17: "expect more coercions to come on line as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric hierarchy" (`128f313b5`). Steele added the prelude's `Comparison` traits with their `extends` clauses commented out on 2011-07-15 (`b3c2e1342`) and added the operators of the sibling `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` on 2011-07-22 (`da5291587`). Steele's 2016 slide draws `Number → {Integral → ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ; Float → RR32, RR64}` (`SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:159-161`).
31	- Rounding: the draft's rational chapter declares `floor`, `⌊⌋`, `ceiling`, `⌈⌉`, `round`, `truncate` all returning ℤ, and says `round` sends an exact half to the even integer (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:457-472`). It has no chapter for the floating-point types. The 2008 release, in its library listing, declares for floats what C and IEEE do: `floor(a: Number): RR64`, `⌊a⌋: ZZ64`, `ceiling(a: Number): RR64`, `⌈a⌉: ZZ64`, `truncate(a: Number): ZZ64` (the 1.0 PDF, pdftotext lines 8295-8299). The interpreter's api declares the same on `RR64`: `floor(self): RR64`, `|\self/| : ZZ64`, `ceiling(self): RR64`, `|/self\| : ZZ64`, `truncate(self): ZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:368-372`); its component body is inconsistent with the api (`|\self/| : ZZ`, `truncate(self): RR64`, `round(self): ZZ`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:470-475`). The team's prelude declared none of them for `RR64` and left `floor(self): RR64` and `ceiling(self): RR64` in a comment (`git show 5a68404fd:ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi`, lines 438-439).
32	- Overflow: "For integer results, overflow throws an `IntegerOverflow`" (`basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`), kept by Steele in the 2012 restart; wrapping has its own operators ∔ ∸ ⨰ and saturation ⊞ ⊟ ⊡ (`:172-176`, `:205-209`). The interpreter wrapped silently; Maessen's 2007 comment calls the range checks not yet done.
33	- Where they left it open: how to have both the exclusion rule (below) and ℤ inside ℚ. Naden, 2012: the numeric hierarchy is written with the self-type idiom, it has "crossed instantiations of the kind that we determined must be outlawed", the self-type bound fixes one failure and not the other, "Victor and John have started working on this sort of theory with their trolls", and "more work needs to be done in order to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:568-632`). Nobody solved it.
34	
35	### Generics and their specialisation
36	
37	- A **static parameter** is a parameter of a declaration filled at compile time or at run time: a type (`List[\T\]`), a number (`Vector[\T, nat n\]`), a boolean, an operator, a dimension. An **instantiation** fills it (`List[\ZZ\]`). Fortress **reifies** generics: a value carries its instantiation at run time, so dispatch can tell `List[\Boolean\]` from `List[\String\]` (Steele 2016, slide 41). Java erases them; this is where Fortress departed from Java.
38	- **Specialisation** is a generic declaration beside a special version for one instantiation: `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\])` beside `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])`, chosen at run time by the value. Naden's 2011 workshop paper says the library's authors "found it useful ... to define both monomorphic and polymorphic versions of functions" (`reviews/mie-probes/literature.md` § 1). The team's tests and the checker's dispatcher are built for it.
39	- To make that sound they adopted **multiple instantiation exclusion**: no type may be a subtype of two different instantiations of one generic ("a rule that forbids multiple instantiation inheritance, in which a type (other than Bottom) is a subtype of distinct applications of a type constructor", `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`; in the checker since 2010-05-28 and as `checkP` since 2010-07-26). The 2012 Types chapter renames it "instantiation exclusion" and adds a `covariant` modifier (`types.tick:322-339`, `:353-372`). Naden: "Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`). The tower breaks it because each level says "I am `Equality` at my own type", so one `ZZ32` is `Equality` at five instantiations.
40	- **Run-time instantiation**: when dispatch picks a generic declaration the static call did not select, its parameters must be inferred at run time; the 2011 paper says so and leaves how "beyond the scope of this paper" (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`). Welterweight aims for "the most specific instantiation of an applicable entrypoint" (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:67`). Steele's 2016 slide 44, "Where We Got Stuck": generic methods with symmetric dispatch need the parametric meet rule and the return-type rule, which need "nontrivial run-time constraint solving" ("a euphemism for exponential cost"); "So we had a grand vision, but could not quite pull it off." Naden's last memo (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/`) restricts the instance by the static return type; implemented on neither path.
41	- **`where` clauses**, a second way to bind a type variable ("Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves", `basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-352`, and `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`, `:384-397`): "Widening and where clauses are not yet supported" (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:15`); code generation refuses any declaration with one (FACTS:158).
42	
43	### Overloading and dispatch
44	
45	- Fortress has **symmetric multimethods**: an overloaded call is resolved on all its arguments, once statically (the most specific declaration applicable to the static types) and again at run time (the most specific applicable to the run-time types, `basic/overloading.tex:262-276`). The **return-type rule** ties the two: a more specific declaration's result must fit the less specific one's, so the run-time choice never returns something the static choice did not promise.
46	- On static parameters the 2008 release had a first model that "may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine are implemented" (the 1.0 PDF, lines 5234-5241). The 2009 draft replaced it with a ban: "it is an error for their static parameters to differ ... Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`basic/overloading.tex:100-107`), and in the same draft listed "Relaxing restrictions on static parameters of overloaded functionals" as future work with Jan Maessen's `array1` pair (`appendices/future.tex:236-266`). The 2011 paper allows differing static parameters under three rules (No Duplicates, Meet, Return Type), the checker enforces them, walk never enforced the ban, and the 2012 restart drops the sentence.
47	
48	### Coercion
49	
50	- A **coercion** is a conversion a trait declares from another type (`trait ZZ64 ... coerce(z: ZZ32)`), inserted by the compiler where no declaration applies without it. It is not chained (`conversions-coercions.tex:127-130`). "For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are explicitly added" (`:454-462`). It is resolved on static types: "Notice that coercion is resolved statically", with an example where `c: C = D` and `f(c)` calls `f(A)` by coercion "despite the fact that the declaration f(B) is applicable to the dynamic call f(D)" (`:598-635`). The draft's own example of widths declares `ZZ64 coerce(z: ZZ32)` and `ZZ128` from both (`:549-565`); no sentence makes `ZZ32` a subtype of `ZZ64`. "Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values" (`:64-66`), a general sentence.
51	- Numerals: "numerals have their own types ... This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`); the types named (`NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`) carry the value and were never implemented; a note says "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy" (`:83-95`). The prelude has one `IntLiteral`, a sibling each number type coerces from (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390-429`; Maessen 2009: "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec"). The interpreter's is `object IntLiteral extends { ZZ32 }` with its arithmetic commented out: "Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals." (`FortressBuiltin.fss:497-498`).
52	- The prelude's coercions are every exact integer pair and none from an integer into a float (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md` § 5, checked at `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-108`, `:147-149`, `:433-435`).
53	
54	### Sizes
55	
56	- A **`nat` parameter** is a static parameter that is a number: `Vector[\T, nat n\]`. "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values. A nat parameter may be used ... to appear in any context that a variable of type ℕ32 can appear" (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:78-90`). The library's arrays and matrices carry their sizes this way and their products require the inner sizes to agree (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1680-1684`). The team's checker never checked them ("Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"), the code generator reserved a slot for them (`CodeGen.java:5317-5328`), and the library's `NatReflect.fss:38-40` says of making a size from a run-time number "Really this just proves that it can be done without extending the language. Having proven that, we ought to build it in".
57	- Unboxing (storing a float as a machine double, not as an object) was intended and never built: `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:12-19` and the loader's empty "expando" stub (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`).
58	
59	### `comprises` and exclusion
60	
61	- **`excludes`** declares that two traits share no value; an object type excludes every type not above it (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:212-224`). Exclusion is what lets the checker prove two overloads never both apply.
62	- **`comprises`** closes a trait: `trait Number comprises { RR64, QQ, AnyIntegral }` lists the types below it. The draft reads the list at the level of types: the listed traits "are exactly the traits that immediately extend T" (`basic/traits.tex:231-234`, a draft note). The 2012 texts read it at the level of values: an instantiation "is covered by the union of the types in this set" (`types.tick:384-389`); "no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of the comprised types" (`Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:21-22`). The draft's future-work list says "We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check" (`appendices/future.tex:285`).
63	- The **self-type idiom**: `trait Ring[\X\] comprises X`, so `Ring[\ℚ\]` "is really just ℚ itself" (Naden, `:576-582`); the patents of 2012-08-31 make it a named exception to the exclusion rule ("Self-types meet"), never built.
64	
65	### The libraries
66	
67	- The specification knows one library, "chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/library/structure.tex:15-18`). The compiler prelude was cut on 2008-12-19 as a "Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (`WellKnownNames.java:110-111`) and grown for three and a half years; the team called what went into it "bogus" (2009).
68	- The library's own flavour: algebra traits (`AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`, `StandardTotalOrder[\T\]`), each self-typed, carried by every number type; reductions licensed by associativity and identity; open marker traits (`AnyMaybe`, `AnyList`) with a "not yet" comment where a `where`-clause `comprises` was wanted (`FortressLibrary.fsi:434`). The specified algebraic-constraints library (monoids, groups, rings, fields, `HasIdentity`) exists only commented out (`Library/incomplete/`). Steele's 2016 slide 12 promised "Rational, complex, and quaternion"; only rational shipped.
69	
70	### Where the designers left the question open, in one list
71	
72	- Both the exclusion rule and the nested tower (Naden's "more work needs to be done").
73	- Run-time instantiation of a dispatched generic (the 2011 paper's "beyond the scope"; Naden's unfinished memo).
74	- Inference of static arguments at a call (`basic/inference.tex` is a 27-line stub).
75	- A numeral's type hierarchy ("We need to describe").
76	- The float types' rounding methods (no chapter; three inconsistent spellings in their own library).
77	- Whether `comprises` is read on types or on values (two readings, the later one on values).
78	- `where` clauses and widening (never supported).
79	- Sizes in the checker and at run time (a "Todo", a reserved slot, "we ought to build it in").
80	- Which integer width a range has (no sentence; the prelude says `ZZ32`).
81	
82	## 2. The decisions, one by one
83	
84	Three verdicts are used. **Faithful**: the designers' latest word says this. **A call**: the designers left no word; consistent or not with his principles. **A departure**: against the designers' latest word; justified or not. For anything judged wrong: what it has cost, and what reversing it costs now.
85	
86	### F1. The goal and its measuring stick (2026-09-16)
87	
88	- Verdict: a call, and the right frame. Two corrections to its wording. "The July 2012 draft" names the right tree and the wrong date: the team's text is of 2010-12, and it is now revised in place, so "judged by `Specification/`" reads partly the revival's own words (25 revision sections, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`). Answer 1 (2026-09-26) got the citation right, "the Working Draft of February 2011"; the goal's sentence in CLAUDE.md and POSITIONS:24 has not caught up.
89	- Citation: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` §§ 2, 4; FACTS:143.
90	- Cost: none in the work; a reader is misled about when the text was written. Fix: one sentence.
91	
92	### F2. The library's own practice is the standard (2026-09-19)
93	
94	- Verdict: a call, consistent with principle 1 ("custodians, not authors"). It is also the ground on which two of his decisions should have been made and were not (D6's row 330, D23's decision 2). Where it pulls against route A (the practice was the nesting), his yes of 2026-09-24 settled that the practice is the library's patterns, not every one of its shapes.
95	
96	### F3. The later, implementation-informed word outweighs the early text (2026-09-23, 2026-09-26)
97	
98	- Verdict: a call, and the right one for this language, whose draft says one thing in its types chapter and another in its library chapters. Its limit, which the exclusion brief named: it ranks texts by date and by whether they ran, and the two implemented halves (the interpreter's nested library, the compiler's flat prelude and rule) are both the group's. Where it leaves a judgement he made one (D4).
99	- Citation: `reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md:127-131`.
100	
101	### D1. One library, the interpreter's (2026-09-20, 09-21)
102	
103	- Verdict: faithful. The specification names one library; the split's own comment calls it a temporary hack; nothing on record argues for two as a destination.
104	- Citation: `library/structure.tex:15-18`; `WellKnownNames.java:110-111`; `coordinator/library-route-judgement.md` § 1.
105	- Cost: the price is the route itself. Every checker error on the interpreter's library became path work: 1.7K errors on 2026-09-27, 627 now (FACTS:56). The part not yet designed is the destination's last step, the switch-over (section 3, O1).
106	
107	### D2. Sizes in the types and unboxed `double[]`, together (2026-09-19); row 40 closed with no decision (2026-09-25)
108	
109	- Verdict: faithful to the design, which put sizes in types and intended unboxing, and never built either on the compiled path. Closing row 40 as "no decision taken" was right: the worker's three defaults were refuted by probe.
110	- Citation: `basic/trait-parameters.tex:82`; `Unbox.java:12-19`; `NatReflect.fss:38-40`; `reviews/array-design-review.md:13-37`.
111	- What it will cost him: the array review's first finding stands. The model's arrays are unsized in its own types, so on the compiled path "the model's text is the notation" and "sizes are central" collide on every operator application. Decision D's diff measures the collision: 21 model lines out, 29 in, no operator changed, 24 own errors to 12 (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md` § 1), and it is stale since `tabulate`. This is his decision to take with the diff in front of him, not a repair (section 6, item 6).
112	
113	### D3. The scalar-extension block, `AnyAdditiveGroup`, `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` (2026-09-21)
114	
115	- Verdict: a call, approved as landed; the closure was held until measured, which was right. The block is the revival's invention argued from `Number` membership rather than from the algebra the library gives arithmetic (Astra's point; `reviews/batch-6-conformance.md:90`). It blocked the library's own open-marker way when `AnyIntegral` came back (D24). Not wrong; a reminder that phase 5's array bodies need capability bounds, not `Number`.
116	- Citation: `reviews/library-scalar-extension-review.md`; `reviews/anyintegral-comprises-judgement.md` § 2, way 1.
117	
118	### D4. Route A: keep the rule, flatten the tower, teach walk coercion (2026-09-24)
119	
120	- Verdict: faithful to the designers' latest implemented word, and justified. This is the decision the evidence author asked to be looked at hardest, so the reasoning in full:
121	  - For the rule: it is the group's implemented and published position (2010 checker, 2011 paper, 2012 Types chapter, Naden's "blanket" sentence, POPL 2019).
122	  - For the flat tower: the compiler side chose and built it in 2009 and 2010 (Chase, Ryu, Maessen, Allen), and Steele built its operators on it in 2011; the draft's own types chapter says the numeric types are "mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them", and the 2012 Types chapter repeats it; Steele's 2016 slide draws it flat; every high-performance peer he named (Julia, Swift, Rust, X10) is flat with explicit or coerced widening.
123	  - Against: the library chapters' prose and the interpreter's library, both 2008, never checked; Naden's aim to keep both, which he left unsolved; the patents' forest rule, never built, whose soundness rule the revival would have had to write itself (route C, built as a shadow: 188 lines in 5 files, a return-type rule of ours, the interpreter overflowing on `comprises T`, FACTS:48).
124	  - On "the mutually exclusive sentence": the route-A notes cite ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ as what the specification states and do not cite this sentence (`reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md:39`; the flattening note cites both, `reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md:181`, `:454`). Had the brief cited it, his case would have been stronger, not weaker: the specification's types chapter, the later of its two voices, already said what route A does. The revised number chapters now agree with it (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, the `revival-rationals` callout).

1	<!-- The recheck of `judgement.md` (2026-09-29, `9172ab41f`) against the full text of Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance", PACMPL 3 (POPL 2019), article 11, 28 pages, read whole from `research/decks/popl19w.txt` (pdftotext of `research/decks/popl19w.pdf`; both gitignored, neither committed). 3	# The POPL 2019 paper against the judgement: what changes
4	
5	## In short
6	
7	- The paper confirms the large calls: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat, the 2009 overload sentence gone, the three rules, the return-type rule in the form batch 7b's rung C plans, applicability and specificity on declared quantified domains, and the implicit bound `Any`.
8	- It contradicts one default and one mechanism, both in batches not yet run or cheap to change: item 30's "least instance" is the 2012 rule the paper says the team could not prove and abandoned; the checker's binding of an unconstrained type parameter to `Bottom` (rows 447, 425, 516) is what the paper's model forbids outright. The paper's rule for both is the same sentence: instantiate at the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the call's static return type, never at the value's type alone and never at `Bottom`.
9	- It adds four things the record lacked: that rule; the exact form of the overloading rules with "existential reduction"; a restriction that its proof needs (a method type parameter may not appear in another's upper bound), which the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families break; and a phase-5 requirement, that the dispatcher must know the call's static return type at run time.
10	- Three things should be done differently, all cheap: item 30's sentence in 7b's rung S and one test pair in rung C; the `Bottom` binding replaced by the bound in one checker rung, which replaces the "treat as a throw" fix the judgement recommended for row 447; row 516's union replaced by the bound. Nothing on route A, answer 9, item 26 or the conversion order changes.
11	
12	## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says
13	
14	The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:
15	
16	- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
17	- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
18	- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
19	- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
20	- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
21	- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
22	- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
23	- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
24	- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).
25	
26	## 1. The verdicts the paper bears on
27	
28	### 1.1 Route A: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flattened (D4)
29	
30	- The paper confirms the rule and the flattening. [Anc-Same-Trait] is the exclusion in the paper's own terms, and "because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait" (p. 11:11, lines 550-554). There is no tower, no self type and no `comprises T` in it (searched).
31	- It adds one thing the route-C notes could not know: variance cannot rescue the tower. The self-typed algebra traits put their parameter in a parameter position (`opr =(self, other: T)`), and [D-Method] forbids a covariant parameter there (lines 571-572, 584-592). So `Equality[\+T\]` is ill formed, and the covariant clause of the ancestor rule, the only clause that admits two instances on one chain, is closed to the tower. The patents' forest rule stays what the record called it, a sketch outside the group's proven model.
32	- Nothing to do differently. One line for batch 7b's rung S: Appendix I's instantiation-exclusion entry cites [Anc-Same-Trait] beside the 2011 paper and the 2012 Types chapter.
33	
34	### 1.2 Answer 9: the overload sentence goes, the three rules, the return-type rule over every instance (D17)
35	
36	- The paper confirms the drop and the rules: a generic declaration "is applicable to a type α if there exists an instance D of d that is applicable to α" (§ 2.2, p. 11:5, lines 246-248); "we use the subtype relation of their domain types as in Allen et al. [2011]" (§ 4.1, line 604); the three rules as Figure 5 states them.
37	- It confirms rung C's planned form of the return-type rule. The record plans "the paper's special arrow, `∀[Δ1, Δ2] (S1 ∩ S2) → T2`, with the less specific declaration's parameters kept quantified except where the domain reduction forces an equality" (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md:93`); that is [Return-Test] with the paper's reduction in a narrower form.

Cost: one paragraph and one test in a rung already in batch 7b.

42

Type parameters are α-renamed ("We assume the conventional α-conversion to rename bound variables", line 669) and a dispatched declaration is instantiated by substitution from the ilks and the static return type ([Dispatch], line 874-879), never handed the call's written static arguments by position. It guards an implementation habit, not a rule of the designers' model. It refuses nothing in the library (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7.md:234`).

Cost: wording in an entry rung S already writes.

48	
49	- The paper has no coercion, so it is silent on the order "convert only when nothing fits". It confirms the two halves the decision rests on: applicability when some instance fits (line 246-248) and specificity on declared, quantified domains (line 604, Figure 6).
50	- It adds a caution about what its proof covers. Its well-formedness rule (2), "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" (lines 565-570), excludes every F-bounded generic function: the library's `SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]` and `PROD` of answer 7, its `BIG MAX[\T extends StandardMax[\T\]\]`, and every function over `T extends Integral[\T\]`. Theorem 4.1 (§ 4.3, p. 11:15, lines 782-789) keeps static uniqueness: No Duplicates makes the more-specific relation antisymmetric, Meet makes every applicable set a meet semilattice, and "there always exists a unique most specific method declaration". Rung S's entry for the proof appendix says in one sentence that FGFV keeps static uniqueness as a theorem, that the coverage case is beyond FGFV, and that the revival gives up static uniqueness there on the addendum's premises. The record chose "the instance the value fixes, the least instance where it fixes none", Welterweight's rule (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:189-192`: "l_j is the type inferred for P_j", the lower bound), and recorded Naden's return-type restriction as future work, weighing Naden's 2012 objection that programmers could not follow execution without static types (`literature.md` § 1). 68
